Why Do Cicadas Count In Prime Numbers?

biology 12 Aug 2026

Sentence34 words · 0.2 min

Periodical cicadas stay underground for exactly 13 or 17 years — both prime — because a prime cycle is the hardest possible rhythm for a predator, or for another cicada brood, to synchronise with.

Under the eastern United States, several billion cicada nymphs are drinking root sap and waiting — for 13 years, or for 17. Then, over a few nights, they climb out together at densities above a million insects per acre. The synchrony is the defence: no predator can eat more than a fraction of such a glut. The numbers matter too, because 13 and 17 share no factors. A predator booming every two or three years can almost never line its good years up with theirs. The insects are not doing arithmetic. Selection did the arithmetic, and the survivors are the broods whose counting landed on a prime.

Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground and emerge all at once. The strategy is called predator satiation, and it is blunt. A cicada is slow, loud, defenceless and delicious; alone it has no chance. In a swarm so dense that birds, raccoons, squirrels, fish, snakes and cats stop eating before the supply runs out, the population survives by exhausting appetite itself. That needs near-perfect synchrony — a cicada a year early is a snack, not a horde — and it needs rarity, since a predator that could count on the feast would grow to meet it.

That is where the primes earn their keep. Imagine a predator whose own population peaks every four years. A 12-year cicada cycle would coincide with it every single time. A 17-year cycle coincides once in 68 years. Any cycle with many factors is easy to intercept; a prime is caught only by the full period. The same logic separates the cicadas from each other: a 13-year and a 17-year brood share an emergence once every 221 years, which keeps them from blurring together through hybrids with useless intermediate timing.

What no one fully understands is how a blind insect underground keeps count. It is not a simple internal clock: cicadas shift by exactly four years — never one, never two — appearing as stragglers ahead of or behind their brood. The best evidence points to the trees. Nymphs feed on xylem fluid, whose composition changes as the host leafs out and goes dormant, and cicadas moved onto peach trees forced to flower twice in a year emerged a full year early. They count seasons through their food, then wait for the soil to reach about 18 °C.

The waiting

An adult female periodical cicada cuts slits into the pencil-thin twigs of a tree and lays her eggs inside. Six to ten weeks later the hatchlings drop to the ground like grains of rice and burrow. They will not see daylight again for well over a decade. Underground, a nymph attaches to a rootlet and drinks xylem fluid — a diet so dilute in nutrients that it partly explains the leisurely development. It moults through five instars, moving deeper and then, in its final years, back toward the surface.

The trigger

Emergence is coordinated by soil temperature. When the ground about 20 cm down warms to roughly 18 °C, usually after a soaking rain in late spring, the nymphs come up over a few nights. They climb the nearest vertical thing, split their nymphal skin down the back, and pull themselves out white and soft, hardening over the next hours into black-bodied, red-eyed adults. The abandoned shells stay stuck to bark, fence posts and porch furniture for months.

The noise

Male cicadas sing with tymbals — ribbed membranes on the abdomen that buckle like the lid of a tin can, thousands of times a second, amplified by a mostly hollow abdomen. Massed choruses reach 90–100 decibels, roughly a passing motorcycle, and each of the seven Magicicada species has its own song, which keeps the species from interbreeding even when they emerge in the same week from the same lawn. Interested females answer with a precisely timed flick of the wings. Adults live four to six weeks, mate, lay eggs, and die in drifts that fertilise the forest floor with a pulse of nitrogen the trees measurably respond to.

Why so long, and why prime

Two questions hide inside the life cycle: why so many years, and why these particular years. The long cycle is usually explained by climate history. Periodical cicadas evolved through the Pleistocene, when cool summers made development slow and unreliable; a very long juvenile stage buffered against bad years, and one great synchronised gamble beat many small ones. Given a long cycle, prime lengths win the arithmetic. They minimise how often the swarm collides with cyclical predator peaks, and they minimise how often broods of different lengths meet and hybridise — hybrid offspring inherit intermediate timing, emerge out of step with everyone, and are eaten.

The broods

The cicadas are organised into broods: regional populations that emerge in the same year. Brood X covers much of the mid-Atlantic and Midwest; Brood XIX, a 13-year brood, sweeps the South. Adjacent broods are offset by a year or a few, so somewhere in eastern North America there is nearly always a brood emerging. In 2024, the 13-year Brood XIX and the 17-year Brood XIII overlapped in Illinois for the first time since 1803 — a genuine 221-year event, and a reminder that the numbers on which the whole system rests are the ones with nothing in common.

A very slow animal

There are thousands of cicada species worldwide, and nearly all of them are what entomologists call annual or proto-periodical: they take two to eight years to develop, but their generations overlap, so some adults appear every summer. Only one group, the genus Magicicada of eastern North America, has gone to the extreme of a rigidly synchronised, decade-plus cycle. Seven species are recognised, split into three groups by song and morphology — decim, cassini and decula — and each group has both a 17-year northern form and a 13-year southern one.

The underground life is the bulk of it. After hatching, a first-instar nymph must find a rootlet before it desiccates. It taps into the xylem — the plumbing that carries water and dissolved minerals up from the roots — rather than the sugar-rich phloem that aphids exploit. Xylem fluid is almost pure water with traces of amino acids and minerals, and drinking it requires enormous suction and specialised gut bacteria to supply the amino acids the diet lacks. Growth is correspondingly slow. Nymphs pass through five instars, digging deeper in the early years, then constructing a chimney or cell near the surface in the final one, waiting for the season.

Density is the striking part. In a good stand of mature hardwood, emergences of 1.5 million cicadas per acre have been recorded — a biomass comparable to a herd of cattle standing on the same ground, quietly extracted from tree roots over 17 years and released in a fortnight.

Satiation as a strategy

Most prey animals invest in escape: speed, camouflage, toxins, vigilance. Periodical cicadas invest in none of these. They fly badly, blunder into people, are conspicuously black and orange, and taste, by all accounts, fine. Their entire defence is arithmetic — appear in numbers so far beyond what local predators can consume that the survivors are simply the ones nobody got around to.

For satiation to work, three things must hold. Emergence must be tightly synchronised, because a trickle of early or late individuals feeds predators without saturating them. The interval must be long relative to predator population dynamics, so that no predator can build its numbers on the expectation of the feast — a bird cannot raise 17 years of extra chicks in advance. And the population must be locally dense, since the strategy is regional, not continental.

Field studies confirm the shape of the effect. During an emergence, bird predation on other prey collapses, because birds switch to cicadas; some bird populations show a boost the following year and a dip afterwards. Nest predation on songbirds falls. In the year after an emergence, forest soils show a nitrogen pulse, and tree growth changes measurably — first suppressed by the egg-laying damage that leaves twig tips brown and hanging (“flagging”), then boosted by the fertiliser of several tonnes of dead insects per hectare.

The number theory of staying alive

Suppose cicadas have a fixed cycle of n years, and suppose there exists some predator, parasite or disease whose own abundance peaks every k years. The two coincide every lcm(n, k) years. If n is 12 and k is anything from the set {2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, the coincidence is total: every emergence meets a peak. If n is 17, then unless k is itself 17, coincidence only occurs every 17k years. A prime cycle is maximally evasive, and it is evasive against every short cycle at once.

The second, and probably stronger, version of the argument concerns cicadas themselves. Broods with different cycle lengths that occasionally emerge together can hybridise. Offspring with intermediate or mixed timing break the synchrony that satiation depends on, and are removed by predation. Selection therefore favours cycle lengths that meet other cycle lengths as rarely as possible — again, primes. Mathematical models of populations with mixed cycle lengths, run over evolutionary time, reliably converge on 13 and 17 rather than 12, 14, 15, 16 or 18. The result is a rare case where an abstract property of a number has a visible ecological consequence.

There is a caveat worth stating. No one has ever identified the specific cyclical predator the 17-year clock supposedly evades, and modern predators of cicadas — birds, mammals, fish — are generalists without strong multi-year cycles. The prime hypothesis is best supported by the hybridisation argument and by evolutionary modelling, not by a smoking-gun parasite. Biology is full of adaptations that answer a pressure that no longer exists.

How they count

The most alien detail is the counting. A nymph in the dark for 17 years must know the difference between year 16 and year 17, and it must agree with millions of its neighbours over hundreds of kilometres.

The clues come from mistakes. Cicadas do stray from schedule — but by exactly four years, early or late, and almost never by one, two or three. That quantisation suggests the count is not a continuous accumulation but something structured, with a switch that can be thrown four years off. Some researchers propose a developmental gate: a nymph must reach a certain size or stage by a certain season, and missing it defers the emergence by a fixed block of years.

The seasonal signal itself is most likely the tree. In an experiment on 17-year cicadas transplanted onto potted peach trees, trees induced to flower twice in a single calendar year produced cicadas that emerged a year ahead of schedule — strong evidence that the insects register the host plant’s annual rhythm through the fluid they drink, rather than through any internal calendar of their own. The final go signal is physical: soil temperature at nymph depth crossing about 18 °C, which is why an emergence rolls northward across a state over a couple of weeks and why a warm rain sets off the night everyone remembers.

Four-year stragglers are also how new broods are probably born. If enough individuals shift together, they can found a population that emerges four years off from its parent, and if that population is dense enough to satiate predators on its own, it persists. The map of broods across eastern North America — numbered in Roman numerals, some vast, some down to a few counties and fading — is a record of exactly this: a slow, error-driven radiation, running at one generation per human generation, still going on underneath the lawns.
